Complaisance is the quality or habit of being too eager to please others — a disposition to go along with what other people want, even when it means setting aside your own preferences, opinions, or better judgment. It describes a tendency to accommodate, agree with, and yield to others in order to keep them happy or to avoid conflict.

Think of it as the opposite of being assertive. A person with complaisance doesn't push back. They fold. They agree. They adjust themselves to fit whatever the other person seems to want.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Imagine a friend who is asked for their honest opinion on your business idea. Instead of telling you the truth — that the plan has serious flaws — they smile and say, "Sounds great!" They don't want to upset you, so they simply tell you what you want to hear. That pattern of behavior, that consistent habit of prioritizing another person's comfort over honesty or one's own stance, is complaisance.

Or picture an employee who never disagrees with their boss — not because the boss is always right, but because the employee simply doesn't like conflict and wants to appear agreeable at all times. Again, that's complaisance.

Or think of a diplomat who, in a negotiation, keeps giving ground and making concessions just to maintain a pleasant atmosphere, even when doing so harms their own side's interests. That excessive agreeableness in the name of pleasing the other party is complaisance.

At the heart of complaisance is a strong desire to be seen as pleasant, cooperative, and easy to deal with. It's not just about being polite. It goes further than that — it's about actively shaping your behavior around what you think others want from you, sometimes to a degree that becomes your defining trait.

A complaisant person essentially asks, consciously or not: "What does this other person want, and how can I be that?" Their own preferences, opinions, and judgments tend to come second.
The Connotation: Is It a Good Thing or a Bad Thing?

Complaisance leans negative, though it can occasionally be used in a neutral way.

When used negatively (which is most common), it implies a weakness of character — a lack of spine, a failure to stand your ground, or a pattern of being too easily swayed by what others want. Someone who shows too much complaisance can be seen as a pushover, a yes-man, or someone who cannot be trusted to give you an honest opinion.

That said, in older or more formal writing, you might occasionally see it used in a more neutral or even slightly positive sense, simply to mean "a pleasant willingness to accommodate others." In those cases, it isn't entirely critical — it just describes a cooperative and agreeable manner. But even then, it carries the implication of accommodation going further than mere politeness.

The bottom line: when you use or encounter this word, you should assume it carries at least a mild note of criticism unless the context makes clear otherwise.
The Most Important Distinction: Complaisance vs. Complacency

These two words are extremely easy to confuse because they look and sound similar, but they mean entirely different things.

Complacency (or complacence) is about being smug, self-satisfied, or uncritically at ease with yourself or your situation — so much so that you stop trying to improve or stop noticing problems. A complacent person is overly comfortable within themselves. For example: "After years of success, the company grew complacent and failed to notice that competitors were catching up."

Complaisance, on the other hand, is directed outward — toward other people. It's not about being comfortable with yourself; it's about being overly accommodating toward others.

A simple way to keep them apart:

  • Complacency = too comfortable with yourself
  • Complaisance = too eager to please others

This is the single most important distinction to hold onto, because even educated writers mix these two up.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Compliance means following rules, instructions, or demands — it's about obedience to something specific (a law, a policy, an order). Complaisance is broader and more personality-based. It's not about following one specific rule; it's about a general, ongoing disposition to please.

Deference means respectfully submitting to someone's opinion or authority, usually because you genuinely respect them or recognize their expertise. Complaisance is less about genuine respect and more about a habitual desire to please and avoid friction.

Obsequiousness is complaisance taken to an extreme — it means being so eager to please that it becomes servile, fawning, and even embarrassing. Obsequiousness is complaisance with the volume turned all the way up.

The adjective is complaisant (meaning "inclined to please; agreeably obliging"). Knowing this helps, because you'll sometimes encounter the adjective in texts before or instead of the noun. A complaisant person is one who exhibits complaisance. They are two sides of the same coin.

Here's a mental anchor: the word contains the idea of "comply" + "pleasant." Someone with complaisance is complying in order to seem pleasant. They're reshaping themselves to match what others want, and they do it with a smile. That image — agreeable, accommodating, always saying yes, always softening their own stance to please the room — is the heart of complaisance.
